The Monitor's View The EU moves forward on expansion – and the rule of law To join the European Union, countries need to meet governance and anti-corruption standards. As European citizens also keep pushing for these, a new report finds some evidence of progress. | Jacqueline Jacquemart/©European Union 2025 Albanian Prime Minister Edi Rama and EU Commissioner Marta Kos updating the chart showing Albania’s progress on EU accession negotiations, Brussels, September 2025. Loading... By the Monitor's Editorial Board July 22, 2026, 3:33 p.m. ET The rule of law across Europe is on a “broadly positive trajectory,” according to the just-released 2026 European Commission Rule of Law Report. Reforms that bolster independent justice systems and align anti-corruption rules to continentwide principles are part of this arc. In a global context, where democratic norms appear to be on the back foot and several governments are flexing authoritarian muscles, this is good news. But in a note of caution, the same document also points to uneven progress – particularly among Eastern and Central European countries. The report found that 47% of its 2025 recommendations for improved rule of law had been acted on. Other data shows that citizens in 17 EU countries, and businesses in 18, perceived judicial independence as having improved or stayed stable from the previous year. And despite some evidence of hostility to journalists, the EU-Balkans zone remains in first place in regional rankings in the latest World Press Freedom Index. Alongside these findings, there is a renewed openness to new members joining the 27-country union. Last week, the EU held talks with Albania and Montenegro, which have already completed more than half the requirements to join, and with Moldova and Ukraine, which are only just beginning negotiations. “It’s really a super Tuesday for enlargement,” Le Monde reported EU Commissioner Marta Kos as saying on July 14, the day of the most recent membership discussions. “For more than two decades, we haven’t had four accession conferences in one day.” The last time a new member was added to the EU was 13 years ago – Croatia, in 2013. To overcome this expansion inertia, EU founding nations France and Germany have called for a new process of “structured gradual integration.” This would grant candidate countries some early trade and integration benefits, but would hold off on granting full voting and representation rights until all required structural and governance changes are in place. The prime minister of Albania had earlier indicated a willingness to waive voting and veto rights, to speed up inclusion. EU members are supportive of enlargement, Commissioner Kos noted, “but only if the candidate countries are delivering” on good governance. Her comment points to the stalled membership negotiations with countries including Serbia, Bosnia-Herzegovina, and North Macedonia, over failure to implement reforms. Even EU members such as Slovakia and Hungary have seen declines in rule-of-law indicators. But with April’s decisive popular vote against longtime autocrat Viktor Orbán, Hungary now signals hope for democratic renewal and recovery. “A new, active political generation is beginning to unfold before our eyes,” a Hungarian political analyst told The Associated Press. Its “strong sense of justice,” the analyst said, is incompatible with “the authoritarian exercise of power [and] the corruption.” Deepen your worldview with Monitor Highlights. Already a subscriber? Log in to hide ads . This trend is in evidence across the region, where voting constituencies have consistently protested corruption and called for democratic decision-making in recent years. The citizens of Central and Eastern Europe prize the rule of law as much as the rulemakers in the EU. Both forces, together pushing for transparent, honest governance, will likely be hard to resist in the long run. You've read of free articles. Subscribe to continue. Quake leaves Colombian towns in ruins as Valle del Cauca counts dead Copy/paste the link below: Copy Copy/paste the article video embed link below: Copy Updated: 12/08/2026 - 12:00 GMT+2 Western Colombia hit by deadly quake as Zarzal, Roldanillo and El Cairo report widespread damage. … More In Zarzal, around 700 homes were damaged, with some reduced to rubble. At least one person died, while emergency teams assessed homes door to door to identify residents needing shelter and supplies. Debris blocked streets, and some badly damaged buildings may have to be demolished. ADVERTISEMENT ADVERTISEMENT In Roldanillo, residents returned to damaged streets and businesses to salvage what they could. At least two people died, including councillor Juan Carlos García Castañeda, killed when part of a gym collapsed. Hundreds of homes and businesses were damaged, prompting a state of public calamity and a night-time curfew. With power and running water cut, many families slept outside or in temporary shelters. Traders sifted through the rubble for salvageable goods, facing the loss of their livelihoods. In El Cairo, a town of around 7,000 people near the epicentre, officials said about 80% of homes and public buildings were damaged or destroyed. Landslides, blocked roads and aftershocks have forced many residents into makeshift shelters. The quake, which struck on 10 August, has left communities across Valle del Cauca facing a long clean‑up and an uncertain recovery. Regional officials say at least 27 people have died in municipalities in the department outside Cali, and that more than a thousand homes have been damaged, with assessments still under way. As search‑and‑rescue operations continue in the worst‑affected towns, local leaders warn that restoring housing, services and livelihoods will take months, if not years. Photograph: Esa Alexander/Reuters South Africa At least 27 dead after two mass shootings in South Africa, police say Seventeen people killed at bar near Johannesburg and 10 killed in separate incident at barbecue venue near Cape Town Rachel Savage in Johannesburg and agencies Sun 27 Sep 2026 04.19 EDT Last modified on Sun 27 Sep 2026 05.42 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Two separate mass shootings near South Africa’s two biggest cities killed at least 27 people, police have said. The South African police service said on Sunday that 17 people were killed on Saturday night when eight suspects armed with AK-47 assault rifles and pistols opened fire at a bar in Wedela township, south-west of Johannesburg. At least 15 other people sustained gunshot injuries in that attack, police said. In a separate statement, police said 10 people had been killed in a mass shooting at an entertainment venue selling grilled meat, known as a shisanyama , in Lwandle, near Cape Town. Another 11 people were wounded in that shooting. Police said they were searching for multiple suspects, without giving an exact number. The two attacks happened days after a mass shooting by three gunmen at a house party near the east coast city of Durban killed 11 people, including a pregnant woman. No arrests had been made in the two latest mass shootings, police said. South Africa has struggled with high rates of violent crime for years, but the series of mass shootings this week were shocking even to a country used to some of the highest violent crime rates in the world. Police in the province of Gauteng said on Sunday morning they had launched a manhunt for the unidentified eight suspects in the Johannesburg tavern shooting, with no arrests yet made. “It is alleged that patrons were drinking inside and outside the tavern when the suspects arrived and opened fire on those outside,” a police spokesperson, Capt Tintswalo Sibeko, said in a statement. “The suspects then entered the tavern and continued shooting at patrons inside. The suspects were reportedly armed with AK-47 rifles and pistols. They allegedly searched some patrons and took their cellphones before fleeing the scene in two unidentified motor vehicles. Two vehicles were also set alight during the incident.” View image in fullscreen Members of South Africa's forensic pathology service and armed forces personnel inspect the scene of the shooting at the bar in Wedela. Photograph: Emmanuel Croset/AFP/Getty Images Western Cape police said they had set up a team led by serious violent crime detectives to investigate the Cape Town shooting, in which the gunmen entered the shinsanyama venue at about 1.46am on Saturday night and starting shooting at customers. “Five individuals died on the scene while five others succumbed to injuries sustained after being transported to medical facilities,” the statement said. “Eleven others are receiving medical treatment for injuries sustained … Detectives are hard at work in search of the perpetrators of the shooting incident with no arrests effected yet. The identities of the deceased persons will be released once their next of kin are informed.” In the 12 months to 30 June, more than 22,700 people were murdered in South Africa, according to police data . South Africans are already reeling after the discovery of numerous women’s bodies near Johannesburg’s airport since July, most of which were found in the last few weeks. The killings led to renewed anger about high rates of gender-based violence in the country and has piled pressure on police and politicians to do more about it.
